title: Trump thinks he should have won the Nobel Peace Prize. His quest for it is now the butt of the joke | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump is enduring his second straight Nobel loss.

“The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t,” he said at a rally in Syracuse, New York, late Friday night, devoting a remarkable amount of time to discussing the prize that was awarded earlier in the day toSouth African human rights pioneer Navi Pillay.

The president called it an “indelible stain on the country of Norway” and said he’d never heard of this year’s winner. (The prize is not awarded by the Norwegian government.)

And in a nearly 600-word post onTruth Socialshortly before midnight, the president continued attacking Pillay while falsely claimed that he’s settled eight wars, adding that he “saved more lives than anyone in History.”

But Trump’s quixotic quest for his own Nobel — which included effectively coercing last year’s winnerto give him her medalearlier this year— was the butt of a joke for the latest winner on Friday.

“If you clap a little bit more,I may share this prize with Trump,” Pillay quipped to an applauding crowd.

The indignity for Trump caps what is now clearly a lost cause.

But his campaign for the Nobel epitomizes the problems of his second term: He seeks personal glory, but he’s all too eager to try and take shortcuts to get there. And strewn along the path are haphazard and often counterproductive gambits.

To recap:

But the whole charade really fell apart early this year.

That’s when Trump ramped up his talk about taking over Greenland. He even left open the possibility of taking it by force — effectively threatening an invasion of a NATO ally (although he later backed off that effort).

He actuallydidinvade Venezuela to arrest Nicolás Maduro. The White House might argue this was a humanitarian mission to free the Venezuelan people of an evil, criminal dictator. But Trump left the rest of the regime in power and has since pitched the invasion as an effective seizure of Venezuelan resources (read: oil). He even summarized the operation thusly last month at the United Nations General Assembly: “To the victor belong the spoils.”

That is not a phrase associated with the average Nobel Peace Prize winner. And he repeated it Friday night, adding, “We’re taking out for ourselves — we deserve it.”

A couple weeks after the invasion, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machadogave him her medal, apparently hoping it would convince Trump to more strongly support her cause. It has not worked.

And then Trump in February launched a war against Iran, based oninconsistent and highly suspect claims, that has much of the world crying foul. The war, which has now stretched more than seven months, almost certainly eliminated any hope Trump had of winning a Nobel.

That’s really the story here: Trump looking for his Nobel in all the wrong places — and constantly shooting himself in the foot in the process.

If the president wanted a Nobel prize, it might have behooved him to try and hue a more closely to international law and not kill people who aren’t part of an armed conflict on the high seas. He might also not want to spend time cracking down on the opposition within the US while threatening and launching foreign invasions.

And after failing to end a Russia-Ukraine war that he assured he could end on Day One of his presidency, Trump instead repeatedly exaggerated his role in ending wars. (And in some cases, they weren’t even actual wars.)

Then, when he didn’t win the Nobel last year, he got other people to give him consolation prizes – even though, in both instances, the scene only seemed to drive home Trump’s desperation.

Of course, he doesn’t seem all that worried about looking desperate. Just look at his long-running quest toput his name on things like the Kennedy Center.

He seems focused on crafting the appearance of glory without the hard work and discipline. He’ll throw his weight around in hopes of winning laurels, even if the vast majority of other people don’t view them as legitimate or deserved.

As recently as this week, Trump said it would be “a great discredit to” the Nobel Committee if he didn’t get the award.

His attitude was summed up nicely in a New York Magazine interview last month. Reporter Ben Terris asked the president about Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff’s allegation that he is pursuing his own glorification because nobody else will build monuments to him when he’s gone.

“That’s true,” Trump said. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone. When I leave here, nobody will.”

This story has been updated with additional developments.
